derived.title: Western Balkans — one fixed November window, but it onboards the central banks, so the commercial-bank work is still unbought
derived.claim:
The correction this cycle sharpens the opportunity rather than weakening it. Three markets share one hard date and one technical stack. Kosovo's banks are already being taken through file-format and transaction-limit standardisation across every bank.

November onboards only the central banks. The commercial-bank integration is therefore unscheduled, unfunded and unbought in three markets at once. That work covers the payment hub, 24/7 operations, sanctions screening inside a ten-second window, and key management. Bosnia has the same work under a legal deadline.

One reusable readiness package sold four times is a better use of effort than four country campaigns.
derived.buyer: Commercial banks in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia, plus the ~18 Bosnian banks not yet connected
derived.trigger: Montenegro and Bosnia went live on the shared platform on 20/07/2026, though Bosnia launched with only three banks connected. A second onboarding window is set for November 2026. It onboards the central banks of Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia, not their commercial banks. Bosnia separately has a compulsory participation date of 01/01/2027 under its central bank's rulebook of 10/07/2026.
derived.why_not_visible: Each country row is already an opportunity on its own, so the engine ranks them as separate pursuits. The shared deadline and the shared technical stack are only visible across the rows. So is the fact that the November date does not oblige a single commercial bank.
derived.falsifier: If the three central banks onboard on different technical profiles, the package advantage falls back into separate pursuits. The same happens if the November window slips. Firm per-country commercial-bank timetables are the open item, and none is published.

derived.title: SSM footprint — supervised banks must list their own end-of-life ATM estate by a fixed date
derived.claim:
The compliance duty requires banks to produce the one document a hardware refresh case has always lacked. It is a list of the bank's own end-of-life technology, written by the bank and reviewed by the supervisor, with a timeline for fixing it. ATM and self-service estates that run unsupported operating systems belong on that list, whether or not anyone planned to review them.

Separately, Czechia's four-bank shared network has ~957 of 1,917 machines that cannot take a deposit. Bulgaria's four largest banks have ~1,840 dispense-only sites. Both figures already come from the banks' own data.

The commercial conclusion is to arrive in September with the remediation timeline that the Joint Supervisory Team will be monitoring, rather than to arrive in 2027 with a product.
derived.buyer: The 21 named significant institutions across Greece, Cyprus, Austria, Croatia, Slovenia, Slovakia and Bulgaria — and, through inherited group ICT standards, their CEE subsidiaries
derived.trigger: ECB letter SSM-2026-0301 of 07/07/2026 requires each bank to send a full action plan to its Joint Supervisory Team by 31/10/2026. The structural measures must expressly include 'updating legacy, unsupported or end-of-life technologies'. Plans are being drafted now, in September and October 2026. The annual IT Risk Questionnaire moves to February 2027.
derived.why_not_visible: The ECB letter is typed threat_macro: a supervisory duty with no single buyer and no euro value. The Bulgarian and Czech device-census rows are national opportunities with no regulatory deadline. Neither row shows that a compliance document due on 31/10/2026 is what turns a vague deposit-capability gap into a dated, budgeted programme.
derived.falsifier: If the action plans limit 'end-of-life technology' to core banking and cloud only, and leave out self-service estates as operational assets, the opening closes. Ask one significant institution in September whether ATMs appear in its inventory. The answer can be checked before the deadline.

derived.title: Western Balkans — a November deadline that no domestic regulator is enforcing, affecting banks with no budget for it
derived.claim:
Every EU bank has a home regulator, an RTGS (central bank settlement system) migration project and a budget line pointing at this date. The Western Balkans have none of that. The BIS/CPMI assessment has no entry at all for Serbia, Bosnia, North Macedonia, Montenegro or Kosovo. As a result, nobody has told those banks that the date exists. Their cross-border payments will still be rejected in exactly the same way.

Bosnia's position is more exposed. Its domestic clearing is tied by contract to the EPC rulebook, which pulls an EU date into a non-EU market.

That creates an emergency fix window from September to October. The work is cleaning party data, repairing payments and retuning screening for structured fields. It can be sold to banks that will only find the problem when messages start bouncing.
derived.buyer: Commercial banks in Serbia, Bosnia, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Kosovo, Albania and Ukraine with cross-border correspondent traffic
derived.trigger: SWIFT's 2026 standards release removes unstructured postal addresses from cross-border messages over the 14–15/11/2026 weekend. The EPC retail cut-off moved forward to 15/11/2026 03:30 CET. SWIFT's own material says ~65% of payment messages still carry unstructured addresses.
derived.why_not_visible: The ISO 20022 row covers the whole footprint and reads as an EU compliance item. The Western Balkans rows are about a new instant payment rail going live, which is a different programme with a different sponsor. Neither shows the overlap: the same small change teams face an unfunded external deadline six weeks after their instant-payment go-live.
derived.falsifier: If the region's correspondent banks absorb the change for their counterparties, the local buyer disappears. The same applies if the large group parents (RBI, Intesa, OTP, NLB) fix it centrally for their subsidiaries, leaving only the independent banks. Ask one Bosnian and one Serbian bank in September whether the date is on their plan.

derived.title: Cyprus — the only named digital-euro pilot bank in the footprint that is also a confirmed Printec incumbent
derived.claim:
Bank of Cyprus is the one place where a dated digital-euro pilot lands on an estate where Printec's incumbency is confirmed at source. Teller cash recyclers are now identified as Sesami units across 35 of 54 branches. The confirmed base also includes branch transformation, more than 26,000 managed POS and 132 ATMs.

That turns a footprint-wide forward driver into a concrete, time-limited engagement. The work is a firmware, acceptance and key-management gap assessment across a known device base, carried out while the specifications are still being written. That is also the cheapest moment to influence them.

The confirmed offline scope matters most for hardware, because it needs a secure element that today's terminals do not have.
derived.trigger: The ECB named 36 pilot payment service providers on 14/07/2026, including Bank of Cyprus and JCC. Workstream G5 is writing the ATM and terminal implementation specifications now. The pilot runs in H2-2027 for twelve months. Offline person-to-person payments are confirmed in scope.
derived.why_not_visible: The digital-euro row is typed threat_macro and says plainly that it is not yet a discrete deal. The Bank of Cyprus row sits in the installed-base lane, so it is deliberately left out of every opportunity ranking. Neither lane shows the overlap.
derived.falsifier: If the pilot's device work is limited to JCC as acquirer only, with no ATM or terminal workstream at Bank of Cyprus, the incumbency gives no advantage. The H1 results and the G5 specification drafts will show which case applies. Note also that JCC has just lost the state e-payments contract to VivaBank, which may redirect its own investment.

derived.title: Footprint — the recycler business case can now be built from the banks' own published device data, bank by bank
derived.claim:
Recycler selling (recyclers are ATMs that re-use deposited notes) has always relied on national averages and vendor estimates, which a bank can dismiss. A bank cannot dismiss its own published locator in the same way. The change is from a market argument to an account argument: a named list of that bank's own cash-out-only sites, set against its own published deposit volumes.

UBB disclosed BGN 406m through deposit ATMs, against BGN 2.3bn at branch counters. Serbia's regulator shows ATM deposits up 31.7% by count, while withdrawals grew 0.9%.

The same data also sizes what should not be chased. That is why Česká spořitelna is typed lost rather than pursued.
derived.buyer: Named banks whose own locators or disclosures now quantify the gap: UBB, DSK, Postbank and UniCredit Bulbank; the Czech four-bank pool; AikBank, NLB Komercijalna, Raiffeisen and OTP in Serbia; Erste Croatia and OTP Croatia; Tatra, SLSP and VÚB in Slovakia
derived.trigger: This cycle's bank-disclosure run pulled live locator data across eleven markets in the last days of July 2026. It produced per-bank splits of deposit-capable machines that had never existed before. Bulgaria's big four have ~1,500 dispense-only sites, and the Czech pool has 957 of 1,917. The remaining splits are 457 of 568 at AikBank and 467 of 666 at Erste Croatia. They also include 353 of 460 at OTP Croatia and 102 of 304 at NLB Komercijalna.
derived.why_not_visible: Each country row reads as a national opportunity of ordinary size. None of them shows that the type of evidence changed this cycle across eleven markets at once, from inference to the banks' own machine-readable data. That change is what makes a single reusable business-case template worth building, instead of eleven country pitches.
derived.falsifier: Locator flags are marketing labels, not device inventories. The Czech and Bulgarian shards both warn that 'deposit' tags may under- or over-count. UBB's own two deposit fields disagree by five sites. If a bank's audited count clearly contradicts its locator, the template loses its authority. Ask two banks for the audited figure before the template is standardised.

derived.title: EU-10 — wallets arrive in December 2026 and the bank obligation twelve months later, with seven markets not yet building
derived.claim:
Supply and obligation are twelve months apart. The markets least ready on the supply side are the same ones whose banks will have the least time to build a verifier. A verifier is the software that checks a wallet's identity credentials.

Romania is the useful counter-case. Its tier-one banks have already built chip-ID onboarding against a government interface, so the greenfield onboarding pitch there is closed. The open lane in Romania is chip-read hardware and relying-party key management.

The reusable approach is a verifier delivered as a service. It can be sized for optional traffic, because acceptance is only on the user's request. It should be sold into the seven markets that cannot do it themselves.
derived.buyer: Banks in the seven EU footprint markets with no public wallet sandbox — Bulgaria, Croatia, Czechia, Romania, Slovenia, plus Cyprus and Hungary on unconfirmed paths
derived.trigger: Member States must provide a wallet by 24/12/2026. Private relying parties, including banks, must accept it by 24/12/2027. The amended relying-party register regulation comes into force 11/08/2026. An April-2026 tracker records seven of the ten EU footprint markets with no public sandbox.
derived.why_not_visible: The eIDAS row is footprint-wide regulation with no buyer. The Romanian and Macedonian identity rows are national obligations. None of them shows the twelve-month gap between issuance and acceptance. None shows that seven markets have no sandbox five months before issuance. Together, those two facts define the window in which an outsourced verifier beats an in-house build.
derived.falsifier: If Member States ship wallets with a free national relying-party toolkit, the verifier layer becomes a commodity. Greece's existing state wallet infrastructure suggests this is possible. Only the key-management and screening add-ons would then survive. Watch what each Member State publishes alongside its wallet in December 2026.

derived.title: SEE — the Addiko integration splits into two buying centres, and the larger one is a first-time owner
derived.claim:
Last cycle's read was that the whole five-market integration would be bought in Vienna. That is wrong, and the correction opens a larger opportunity than the original claim.

RBI keeps only Croatia, Slovenia and Austria. There the work is a classic funded merger integration against a EUR 75m envelope, with incumbent group frameworks to displace.

The four Western Balkans banks go instead to Alta Group. Alta already owns Alta Banka Beograd and Alta Banka Bitola, but has never run a six-bank group across four jurisdictions. A first-time owner at that scale has no group vendor framework to fall back on.

The Transitional Services Agreement gives Alta a contractual deadline to build one. It runs for 12 months after closing, with a single 12-month extension. Every shared service must therefore be re-sourced by roughly 2H2028-2H2029.

That is a greenfield platform programme, bought by an owner that must buy it rather than inherit it. It covers core and card consolidation, one cash-automation estate, and one AML and transaction-monitoring platform answering to four regulators.
derived.buyer: Two distinct buyers, not one: RBI group procurement in Vienna with the Raiffeisenbank Austria d.d. integration office in Zagreb for Croatia and Slovenia; and Alta Group d.o.o. of Belgrade for Addiko Serbia, Addiko Sarajevo, Addiko Banja Luka and Addiko Podgorica.
derived.trigger: RBI's offer succeeded on 03/08/2026 at 56.16% of shares subject to the offer (55.55% of total capital). NLB's rival bid failed at 31.22%. RBI's own offer document names Alta Group d.o.o. Belgrade as the onward buyer of the four Western Balkans banks, under a transaction agreement signed 08/05/2026. Additional acceptance closes 03/11/2026. All closing conditions are due by 14/05/2027. Carve-out closing is expected H2-2027.
derived.why_not_visible: The bank-disclosure rows record the takeover result. The jobs rows record the carve-out buyer and the services exit deadline. The per-market rows record each bank's device estate. No single row says that the footprint's largest integration programme has two buying centres with opposite characteristics, one entrenched and framework-bound, the other greenfield and vendor-dependent. No row says that the contractual services-exit date, not the closing date, sets the procurement calendar.
derived.falsifier: If Alta Group extends the Transitional Services Agreement to its full 24 months, it may then simply transfer Addiko's existing vendor contracts instead of re-tendering. The greenfield framing would collapse into a renewal Printec is not party to. Equally, if regulatory or antitrust clearances stall past the 14/05/2027 long stop, the carve-out may not complete in the form described.

derived.title: Romania and Cyprus — two bank mergers put four self-service estates in scope in one quarter, each with a date before decisions are fixed
derived.claim:
Two integrations that no single row connects are running to almost the same timetable. Both are device-heavy rather than software-heavy.

Romania creates the country's #3 bank. It has two overlapping self-service, card and acquiring estates to rationalise, on a budget that is already raised. The practical window to shape scope closes when RBI goes quiet on 23/10/2026, not when the deal closes.

Cyprus is the mirror image. The merged bank has the island's largest ATM fleet, is not a Printec incumbent, and has just published the strongest channel-migration statistic in the footprint. That is the argument for standardising the fleet before the April-2027 core cutover rather than after it.

Treated as one campaign, the two share a reusable proposition and the same eight-week selling window. The proposition is merged-estate rationalisation with a migration-window managed service.
derived.buyer: Raiffeisen Bank Romania merging Garanti BBVA Romania, and Eurobank Limited in Cyprus merging Hellenic Bank.
derived.trigger: RBI's Romanian acquisition is guided to close in early October 2026. Its integration budget of c. EUR 70m is pre-funded by a EUR 600m eurobond raised on 20/08/2026. RBI enters its quiet period on 23/10/2026. In Cyprus, Eurobank Limited disclosed on 06/08/2026 that almost 90% of deposits and 95% of withdrawals now run through machines on a 156-ATM fleet. That is set against a full technical integration targeted for April 2027.
derived.why_not_visible: The Romanian and Cypriot rows sit in different markets and were filed by different shards. Each reads as an ordinary post-merger integration. No row states that both freeze their scope within the same quarter, or that both are decided by device economics rather than platform choice. No row states that one bank has published the deposit-and-withdrawal migration figure the other needs to justify the same investment.
derived.falsifier: If RBI Romania limits the Garanti integration entirely to its existing group frameworks in Vienna, with no local device procurement, the shared window disappears. The same happens if Eurobank Cyprus puts off fleet standardisation until after the April-2027 cutover. In either case these revert to two unrelated pursuits.

derived.title: Hungary — the law that bars banks from removing ATMs turns the national estate into a protected replacement market
derived.claim:
In the rest of the footprint, the commercial question is how fast a bank can shrink its fleet. In Hungary, shrinking the estate is not allowed. The existing estate is commonly put at roughly 5,700 machines, although no cited document carries a verified national total. The law turns that estate from a declining base into a protected replacement base, on top of the 1,039 mandated new rural sites.

Subsection (1b) is the clause that is easy to miss. It accepts that a replacement may not physically fit its predecessor's site. In effect, the legislator has written a site-survey, relocation and enclosure workstream into national law.

OTP and MBH are both reducing their Hungarian estates. OTP Core went from 1,987 to 1,929 ATMs in H1-2026. That is only lawful as replacement, so the activity is happening now.

The market has almost no in-house capability to absorb this work. Only two of sixteen nationwide 'ATM' job hits sit at banks, so the build must be bought in.
derived.buyer: The nine banks carrying Act XVIII allocations — OTP, MBH, K&H, Erste Hungary, CIB, Raiffeisen Hungary, UniCredit Hungary, Gránit and MagNet — with OTP (428 units) and MBH (195/316) carrying the largest tranches.
derived.trigger: Act XIV of 2026, in force since 14/05/2026, bars banks from decommissioning any existing ATM or branch cash-payout point. It does expressly allow replacement. Its subsection (1b) expects that a replacement machine may not fit the original site because of its size and security requirements. Phase 2 of Act XVIII requires an ATM in every settlement above 500 inhabitants, and is due 31/12/2026.
derived.why_not_visible: The regulation rows record a ban, which reads as a limit rather than a market. The bank rows record fleets shrinking, which reads as contraction. The jobs row records no hiring, which reads as nothing at all. Only together do they show a legally protected replacement market that the banks themselves cannot staff.
derived.falsifier: If the MNB issues guidance allowing net decommissioning where another cash-access point exists within a set radius, the protected base shrinks. If the nine allocated banks meet Phase 2 through existing shared-network arrangements rather than new installations, the 1,039-unit figure overstates the addressable build.

derived.title: Footprint — as estates convert to operated contracts, the buyer for software and services shifts from the bank to the operator
derived.claim:
Each estate that converts to an operated contract removes a bank-side hardware buyer. It also creates an operator-side buyer for multivendor software, telemetry, cash optimisation and maintenance.

Printec is Atleos Global Partner of the Year, which is the global title and not the European one previously recorded. That standing is the existing route into the merged entity's channel. Post-close terms are decided in the window before Q1-2027, not after it.

The counterweight this cycle is stronger than before. Asseco Central Europe, Mellon and Česká spořitelna all run on KAL's Kalignite, which Brink's part-owns. The same close that reshapes the channel therefore also consolidates a rival software layer.
derived.buyer: The operators themselves: NCR Atleos and Brink's post-close, Euronet, Mellon, Payten
derived.trigger: Brink's received Indian competition clearance on 22/07/2026 for the $6.6bn Atleos purchase. Closing is targeted around Q1-2027, with the UK authority still outstanding. Euronet's Q2-2026 results of 30/07/2026 show 57,814 installed ATMs and no mention of its unclosed Greek acquisition. That acquisition's scope is now confirmed to include card issuing and three-year payments exclusivity.
derived.why_not_visible: All the component rows are typed threat_macro and read purely as threats: channel risk, account foreclosure, and a rival's software reference. Read together, they describe a buyer moving rather than a buyer being lost.
derived.falsifier: If the merged Atleos and Brink's entity brings services in-house and cuts channel partners after close, the operator-as-buyer route closes rather than opens. The post-close partner and Cashzone strategy is the thing to ask for. The KAL independence question should be put directly to Atleos channel management.

derived.title: Footprint — Printec's ATM supplier changes owner in the same quarter that every supervised bank must list its end-of-life technology
derived.claim:
A bank writing that inventory in October has to decide what happens to an ageing self-service estate. It has to decide at the exact moment when the estate's main supplier is being absorbed by Brink's. Brink's ATM outsourcing line is growing 14% organically, and it has just signed a full outsourcing agreement with an unnamed European bank consortium.

The two facts pull the bank in opposite directions, but they point Printec the same way. Supervisory pressure says refresh or replace. Supplier uncertainty says do not sign a long hardware commitment to a vendor whose ownership changes in ninety days.

The opening is a vendor-neutral end-of-life assessment with a managed-service wrapper. It lets a bank satisfy its supervisor without betting on the outcome of a merger review.

KAL is arguing the opposite case to the same banks. It says a Linux virtualisation layer lets old hardware run a newer Windows and defers the refresh entirely. That argument will happen whether or not Printec takes part in it.
derived.buyer: The SSM significant institutions filing AI-cyber action plans — Alpha, Piraeus, Eurobank, NBG, Bank of Cyprus, Hellenic, Erste Group and its Croatian and Slovak subsidiaries, RBI, BAWAG, UniCredit Bank Austria, NLB, Zagrebačka, PBZ, Tatra, VÚB, Slovenská sporiteľňa, UniCredit Bulbank, DSK and UBB.
derived.trigger: Two deadlines fall together. The UK CMA opened its Phase 1 inquiry into Brink's acquisition of NCR Atleos on 26/08/2026, with a statutory decision deadline of 22/10/2026. Completion was pulled forward to early Q1-2027. Nine days after that decision deadline, on 31/10/2026, every SSM significant institution must file an action plan with its Joint Supervisory Team. The plan must name the institution's 'legacy, unsupported or end-of-life technologies'.
derived.why_not_visible: The regulation row carries a compliance deadline with no vendor angle. The competitor rows carry an ownership change with no bank deadline. The KAL row carries a software pitch. Only the intersection shows that a supervisory filing date and a supply-chain ownership change fall in the same quarter. It also shows that the bank's answer to one is limited by the other.
derived.falsifier: If the CMA clears the merger quickly, and Atleos' European channel terms are publicly reaffirmed before 31/10/2026, supplier uncertainty stops being a reason for a bank to wait. The play then becomes an ordinary compliance sale. Equally, if the action plans limit end-of-life technology to core banking and cloud only, and leave out self-service estates as operational assets, the opening closes.

patterns.Pattern: Cash use is levelling off rather than disappearing. Transactional use erodes ~3-4%/yr, while the amount of cash in circulation and the value of withdrawals hold or rise.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
In the euro area, cash at the point of sale fell from 72% (2019) to 59% (2022) to 52% (2024) by number of payments. It is still ~50% of transactions. Euro cash in circulation hit a record EUR1.59tn (~10% of GDP), and has stayed above 10% for a decade.

ECB counts of card withdrawals fall in every footprint country (RO -1.8%, HU -6.6%, CZ -10.7% over 2yr). The value holds up: Poland ATM withdrawal value rose from PLN104.9bn to 109.1bn from Q4'24 to Q4'25, and Romania was flat at +0.5%. RBR expects CEE withdrawal volume -1.8% CAGR (average yearly change) while value rises +2.7% CAGR (~USD1tn) to 2028.

Crises push demand up: COVID +EUR140bn, the Ukraine invasion +36% in border countries, and the Apr-2025 Iberian blackout. The footprint also stays more cash-heavy. SPACE 2024 puts cash at 56% of spending by value in SI/SK/AT and 51% in Croatia. Albania is still 65% of withdrawal value.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
The installed cash-access base stays useful for much longer than a 'death of cash' view suggests, especially in CEE/SEE.

Sell on cost per transaction for fleets with falling volumes: cash optimisation, OptiCash, recyclers (ATMs that re-use deposited notes) and managed operations. The commercial conclusion is to offer fewer, smarter, higher-value deposit and recycling machines, rather than to expect growth in withdrawals.

patterns.Pattern: ATM fleets sit in three tiers along the EU-maturity line. Mature euro-area fleets shrink ~3-6%/yr, CEE-EU is flat (driven by replacement), and non-EU SEE still grows. The footprint runs ~one cycle behind Western Europe.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
No single ATM strategy fits the whole footprint. The mature tier is a rationalisation and consolidation market, while SEE is a build-out market at the same time. Money for new units and replacements is available now in HU/GR/RO and the Western Balkans.

This gives a multi-year window to sell hardware and to lock in managed services before mature-market shrinkage reaches each country. Tier each market by EU maturity to choose the approach.

patterns.Pattern: Deposit automation and cash recycling are replacing machines within a flat or shrinking fleet. Dispense-only ATMs are being converted to recyclers, which are machines that re-use deposited notes, and this is the one growing hardware segment. The main mechanism is retrofit, not net-new units.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
Globally, more than 50% of ATMs now accept automated deposits. The recycler base is forecast to pass 1.2m by 2029 (~+20%/5yr), described as 'well over half of all ATM shipments worldwide'.

The economics are clear. Cash handling is up to ~50% of TCO. Recyclers cut CIT visits by up to ~80% and give ~20% lower TCO.

Footprint penetration is low and largely untouched outside Russia. Ukraine is only 17.8% deposit-capable, with ~13,000 dispense-only candidates. Serbia has 40 recyclers and Bulgaria 8, and Croatia is only 48% even contactless-capable, against Hungary at 99% and Slovakia at 79%.

Conversion is under way. Albania is 39% deposit-capable with ATM deposits +109% (2025). Kosovo is at 59.4%, up from ~51%. OTP Albania is deploying NCR SelfServ 80, and Tatra banka runs ATM 2.0.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
This is the highest-confidence long-term product line (NCR Atleos recyclers/SelfServ 80). In the footprint, the approach is fleet conversion of large dispense-only bases, such as Ukraine's ~13k and the SEE markets, at a higher value per unit.

Attach software and service to each conversion: x-core multivendor, telemetry and OptiCash. Low current penetration means a long runway.

patterns.Pattern: Owning the ATM channel is separating from running it. ATM-as-a-Service, multi-bank pooling utilities and transfers of bank estates to IADs (independent ATM deployers) are the fast-growing part of an otherwise flat ATM market. The recurring operating layer is moving away from individual banks.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
ATMaaS grows at ~9-12% CAGR and managed services at ~7-10%, against a device market of ~3%, so roughly ~2-3x.

The KAL/ATM Marketplace 2025-26 survey found 19% of banks already fully outsource the ATM network. A further +24% plan to do so within 2yr, nearly doubling into 2027-28. NCR Atleos ATMaaS revenue is up +30-37% YoY (ARR $288m, ATMaaS +33% FY25).

Pooling cuts network cost by up to ~40% and consolidates fleets, as in Sweden (Bankomat 2,700->1,200) and the Netherlands (Geldmaat 6,400->3,800). IADs are ~18% of global ATMs. In CEE, Poland is 64% IAD-deployed and Hungary 16%, which grew fastest.

In the footprint, Euronet took CrediaBank's 141 ATMs (GR), and Atleos ATMaaS went to Epirus Bank. Hungary's Act XVIII legally allows joint installation and operation, which is the precondition for pooling.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Demand shifts from one-off machine sales to multi-year per-device or per-transaction contracts. That is the strongest pull toward Printec's managed-services and ATMaaS line, built with NCR Atleos.

The commercial goal is to own the customer-facing operating contract and to act as the neutral regional operator for emerging pooling utilities. The outcome to avoid is being pushed down to subcontracted field service under a pan-regional IAD such as Euronet, or under Atleos direct.

patterns.Pattern: This is a branch transformation wave over 2024-2026, not branch elimination. Branches are shrinking structurally and the cuts are accelerating, with the steepest cuts in the most recent year. Self-service absorbs the displaced transactions.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
Euro-area offices fell -42%, from ~186k (2008) to ~106k (2023). The EU total fell -3.41% (2024) and then -2.62% (2025) to 122,889, with cuts in 23 of 27 states.

Footprint cuts sped up into 2025: Bulgaria -10.7% (euro-prep year, sharpest in the EU), Slovenia -11.0%, Hungary -9.5%, Romania -7.4% and Czechia -6.9%. Greece is -45% on branches since 2015 while ATMs rose ~17%. Cyprus lost 370 branches and 4,634 jobs (2015-25).

RBR notes that branch-based ATMs fall faster than off-site ones. Off-site machines are 64% of the CEE base and the only growing location band. McKinsey's target is to move >90% of simple activity to assisted or self-service channels.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Each closed teller line or refitted branch turns into self-service demand: recyclers, ITMs/VTMs (interactive and video-teller machines), onboarding kiosks and branch-substitution ATMs.

Higher branch density and later digital adoption put CEE/SEE earlier on the closure-and-transform curve, which gives a durable multi-year cross-sell. Front-loaded closures, such as Bulgaria's euro year, create concentrated replacement demand that can be timed.

patterns.Pattern: The surviving branch is rebuilt around assisted and self-service. Floor space flips from teller-heavy to self-service, and ~80-90% of simple transactions move across. The interactive and video-teller (ITM/VTM) 'branch-in-a-box' becomes the fastest-growing self-service category, and the branch's role shifts to advice.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
McKinsey recommends moving >90% of simple activity to assisted or self-service. It also recommends flipping floor space from ~70% teller to the reverse, and reducing average branch staff (FTEs) from 6 to 4 by 2030.

Vendors are converging on the same model. Diebold Nixdorf Branch Automation (Aug-2025) aims to move up to 80% of teller transactions onto ATMs/TCRs with on-demand video. NCR Atleos ITMs handle ~95% of teller transactions with live video.

The market is growing quickly. The ITM market goes from ~US$1.69bn (2024) to ~US$5.88bn (2033), at ~15.6% CAGR. Video-teller grows at ~17-19.5% CAGR and bank kiosks at ~16% CAGR. Channel proof: Serbia m-banking txns +28% while branches fall.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Demand moves from plain dispense ATMs toward deposit and recycling machines, video-teller machines and onboarding/KYC kiosks.

This frames Printec's offer as turning shrinking branches into fewer, higher-value assisted-service endpoints. The package is hardware, remote-teller software and onboarding, wrapped in managed services, and it is the highest-growth part of the physical channel.

patterns.Pattern: EU payment and resilience rules apply in the euro area first and in the non-euro footprint ~2 years later. The same vendor approach runs again with a built-in lag. That gives a second sales wave on dates that are already known.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
The IPR (Instant Payments Regulation) ladder has two waves. In the euro area, receive applied on 09/01/2025 and send plus VoP on 09/10/2025, which is done in GR/CY/SI/SK/HR/AT.

The non-euro EU countries (CZ/HU/RO) follow later. Receive applies on 09/01/2027. Send-from-EUR and VoP apply on 09/07/2027. Send-from-local applies on 09/06/2028.

VoP (Verification of Payee), the ISO 20022 structured address (14/11/2026) and AMLR (10/07/2027) follow the same euro-first, non-euro-later shape. Euro-area banks bought payment hubs, VoP and 24-7 operations in 2024-25, and CZ/HU/RO must buy the same in 2026-27.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Whatever was sold to Greek, Cypriot, Croatian, Austrian, Slovak and Slovenian banks in 2024-25 can be pitched again to Czech, Hungarian and Romanian banks across 2026-27. That includes VoP, transaction monitoring, ISO 20022 parsing and instant connectivity, with the same propositions and references.

Peak vendor selection for the non-euro tail is H2-2026 to H1-2027.

patterns.Pattern: Each EU regulation runs a fixed cycle. Specifications land ~12-18mo before the deadline, and bank buying clusters 6-12mo before. A higher-margin enforcement and assurance spend then ramps up ~12mo after application. Bank spend can be scheduled years ahead, with a second 'assurance' revenue wave.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
DORA shows the pattern. Batch-1 RTS came in Jan 2024 and applied from Jan 2025. CTPP designation followed, covering 19 providers on 18/11/2025. The TLPT first-cycle deadline is 17/01/2028, with notifications during 2026. It is built into the 2026 SREP/Pillar-2 add-ons.

The EAA applied from 28/06/2025, and market-surveillance audits are ramping up in NL/DE/AT in 2026.

PSD3/PSR was approved by ECON on 05/05/2026. It carries an ~18mo application clock and an ~24mo VoP-liability tail, so commitments run from H2-2026 into 2027. AMLA RTS is due 10/07/2026, and AMLR applies 10/07/2027.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Build the compliance and managed-services pipeline off the sequence of legal deadlines, rather than off discretionary IT budgets.

The high-margin 'year-2' assurance phase is bigger and stickier than the one-off build. It covers resilience testing, incident reporting, TLPT support, EAA remediation and AML/CDD refresh. Sell testing, remediation and managed services in the year after each go-live.

patterns.Pattern: Operational-resilience and financial-crime compliance has changed from one-off 'get-ready' projects into a permanent, legally required running cost. It grows whatever the economy does, and it now reaches into the vendor supply chain through DORA CTPP.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
DORA has been in force since 17/01/2025. The ESAs' first incident report, published 03/06/2026, logged 3,383 major 2025 incidents. About 70% of firms expect permanently higher running costs (McKinsey), and ~22,000 EU entities are in scope.

The cost per institution is EUR 25-150m for large banks and EUR 1-5m for mid-sized ones, which is where most CEE/SEE banks sit. 19 Critical ICT Third-Party Providers were designated on 18/11/2025 under direct EU oversight.

Financial crime adds more cost. Global financial-crime compliance costs USD 206bn/yr (EMEA USD 85bn), and RegTech grows at ~16% CAGR (USD 20.7bn 2025->44bn 2030). National transposition is under way: Romania OUG 14/2026, Greece Law 5193/2025 and Hungary's 'Mini-DORA'.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
This is the rare bank-IT line that is contractually obliged to grow in any economic climate. It is a structural tailwind for Printec's highest-margin security, compliance and managed-services portfolio (INETCO, FICO, IMTF Siron).

Mid-sized CEE/SEE banks cannot staff this in-house, because labour is 72-79% of AML cost, so they outsource. CTPP also means Printec must supply DORA-aligned attestations on its NCR Atleos and managed-services stack to win and keep contracts.

patterns.Pattern: Verification of Payee checks the payee's name before a transfer. Together with ISO 20022 structured data, it turns fraud, AML and identity tooling into a standing, recurring compliance duty rather than project work. The question moves from whether a bank can clear instant payments to whether it can clear them safely, with structured data, at scale.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones): VoP has been a standing legal duty in the euro area since 09/10/2025; non-euro EU by 09/07/2027; the PSR makes VoP mandatory across ALL credit transfers with a ~24mo liability transition. The EPC VoP rulebook keeps updating: v1.0 (05/10/2025)->v1.1 (20/09/2026)->v2.0 (end-Nov 2026). SWIFT CBPR+ structured-address mandate 14/11/2026 (~65% of messages were still unstructured when announced). The PSR shifts APP-fraud liability onto PSPs. Bank readiness gap: only 13% have a strong instant-payments tech foundation, 5% are 'ready to lead'. National instant schemes are multiplying (Greece IRIS mandatory, 4.25m users; Romania RoPay 2.0; Serbia IPS 609k/day; Ukraine SEP 4.1).
patterns.What it means for Printec:
There is recurring, rather than one-off, demand for transaction-monitoring, fraud, VoP and identity lines (INETCO, FICO, IMTF Siron, Namirial). Master-data clean-up projects around the Nov-2026 address cut-off add to this.

The PSR liability shift gives banks a hard, measurable return to justify fraud-analytics spend. Non-euro footprint banks with low readiness approaching the Jul-2027 deadline are the prime 2026-27 pipeline.

patterns.Pattern: EU payment and identity rules flow into the non-EU Western Balkans and Ukraine with a 1-3yr lag. They arrive through SEPA accession and a shared TIPS-clone, which is a copy of the ECB's instant-payment system. The region is repeating the euro area's 2014-17 modernisation on a predictable, pre-set timetable.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
The accession steps follow a fixed order:
- Montenegro and Albania joined SEPA: Nov 2024
- Serbia became the 41st SEPA country: May 2025
- AL/MD/ME/MK joined the schemes: Oct 2025
- Serbian Operational Readiness: May 2026
- Ukraine accession: ~2027-28

Banca d'Italia is building a central switch for AL/BA/XK/ME. It is a TIPS-clone built on ISO 20022, the modern payment-message standard, and should run by ~mid-2026.

Take-up is already visible. North Macedonia is live through 9 banks (Oct 2025). Albania recorded 363k transfers and EUR4.3bn in the first 6mo, with cross-border cost down from EUR73.40 to 6.15. Ukraine has SEP 4.1 instant, UETR mandatory 01/04/2026 and a SEPA bill due ~Jul 2026. The EU Growth Plan (EUR6bn 2024-2027) funds the spend.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
This is a predictable, ordered pipeline of SEPA adherence, ISO 20022 migration and instant-payment connections. It covers Serbia, Albania, N. Macedonia, Montenegro, Bosnia, Kosovo and Ukraine, which is Printec's non-EU home market.

Banca d'Italia builds the central switch, so Printec's value sits on the bank side: connectivity, x-core message transformation, onboarding and acceptance. Get in place market by market, in deadline order.

patterns.Pattern: One-off events create demand spikes with fixed dates. National mandates and euro changeovers go beyond the EU minimum and squeeze years of capital spending into sharp ~6-month local windows. Local laws, rather than Brussels, produce the fastest hardware and terminal spend.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
Greece made IRIS, its instant-payment scheme, mandatory for all businesses, with fines of EUR 10-20k in Nov-Dec 2025. This goes beyond the IPR and forced IRIS into 1.2m POS and ~70k e-shops within months (~122m txns/~EUR11bn in 2025). Greece also added the 11/08/2025 ATM-fee ban/cap.

Bulgaria's euro changeover ran to a fixed timetable. The Commission approved it in Jun 2025. 96% of ATMs were euro-ready by 01/01/2026, with full cutover by 01/02/2026. Free lev<->euro exchange ends 30/06/2026. That packed years of cash-logistics, ATM and core-system spending into ~6 months.

Romania built RoPay ahead of its 2027 dates. Hungary added NIS2/'Mini-DORA' beyond the EU minimum.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
The biggest and fastest bursts of terminal, POS and ATM spend come from national laws and changeovers. Watch national legislation in the footprint, along with ERM-II and convergence signals. Line up stock and integration capacity before the announcement, because the windows are short and the spending is heavy.

Greece IRIS and Bulgaria's changeover are the templates. The next euro candidate and the digital-euro pilots are likely to repeat the same pattern.

patterns.Pattern: IT cost lines are rising, not falling. Cash-in-transit (CIT) and cash-handling costs, compliance running costs and fixed costs per machine are all climbing. This pushes banks to outsource run-and-maintain work and to move spend towards recurring services.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones): Cash handling is up to ~50% of ATM total cost of ownership (TCO); CIT cost +~40% (2020-25); ~75% of ATM operating cost is fixed; cash handling is 4-10% of EU bank operating cost. ~70% of firms expect permanently higher compliance running costs (DORA). Global financial-crime compliance costs USD 206bn/yr and is rising for ~98% of institutions. Banking AI software spend is rising from ~EUR31bn (2024) to ~EUR55bn (2027). Recyclers and pooling cut cash operating cost by up to ~30-40%; recyclers cut CIT visits by up to ~80%. NCR Atleos ATMaaS revenue +33% FY25.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Rising fixed and compliance costs are themselves the reason to buy. Replacing a dispense-only machine with a recycler does more work at a lower cash-handling cost, and pressure on fixed costs pushes banks to outsource.

That is the core case for Printec's recycler line and its managed-services / ATMaaS (ATM-as-a-Service) model. Sell on the cost saving, not on feature lists.

patterns.Pattern: Hardware, cash logistics and payment processing are merging into a few vertically integrated 'end-to-end cash-ecosystem' players. This squeezes pure integrators from both sides.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
There has been a dense multi-year wave of deals:
- Brink's-NCR Atleos $6.6bn (announced Feb-2026, closing Q1-2027, ~$10bn combined company)
- Euronet-CoreCard (Q4-2025) and Euronet-Spain/Portugal (Apr-2026)
- Worldline buying Eurobank's last 20% of Worldline Greece (EUR72m, May-2026)
- Glory-Acrelec (Nov-2025) and Glory-Flooid (2024)
- Loomis-Burroughs (2025)
- Global Payments-Worldpay (Jan-2026)

Each deal combines two or more of {ATM hardware, ATM software, CIT, processing/acquiring}.

Printec's classic role as an independent integrator is being squeezed. Ecosystem players can supply the whole stack themselves and bid end to end.

Printec should move up to owning the customer-facing managed-services contract, together with the local integration and compliance layer, rather than reselling boxes. It also has to choose, deal by deal, which large players to partner with and which to defend against.

Printec's route to market depends on partners whose owners and plans it does not control, and who can cut it out.

Use the Atleos award as leverage to lock in co-sell terms and margin or territory protection now, before the Brink's deal closes and changes the channel economics. Build a spread of suppliers so that one change of ownership cannot strand the business.

Brink's AMS+DRS grew 15% organic for 13 straight quarters. It is about 1/3 of revenue, with ~2/3 of installs greenfield new logos, and Europe is its highest-mix region at 44%. Brink's took a strategic equity stake in KAL (Jun-2025), then agreed to buy Atleos.

Brink's, Mellon and KAL jointly pitched ATM pooling to NBG and Eurobank (Athens, Apr-2026), based on the Lloyds/Brink's UK model.

The CIT layer Printec used to work alongside now competes for the same ATM-lifecycle and retail cash-automation contracts. Where a bank-owned or large CIT controls cash replenishment, the addressable market shrinks. CIT One, for example, blocks BCR/BRD/Raiffeisen ATM-service revenue.

patterns.Pattern: Competition is decided by multivendor software, which runs on any maker's hardware, and by the cost of switching an installed base. The machine itself matters less. Challenger sales models plus deep single-account incumbency create a concentrated, locked-in market.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
Mellon is running a multi-country Hyosung+KAL push: Greece (NBG 700 recyclers 2024), then Bulgaria (Sofia 2024), then Romania (Hyosung+KAL launch 2025). KAL is explicitly hardware-independent, supporting 40+ manufacturers, and is designed to displace incumbents without swapping the fleet.

Payten has been DN's SEE master distributor since 2018, and adds processing (Chip Card) and the MoneyGet IAD. Worldline/Cardlink runs Greece's largest acceptance network (267k POS).
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Winning comes down to which multivendor software and managed-services contract owns the estate. Hardware-agnostic software (KAL vs NCR x-core) converts a fleet without replacing it.

Lead with Printec's multivendor software and services advantage, and defend reference accounts. Where rivals hold the software or processing layer, as with Payten in SEE, JCC in Cyprus and Worldline/Cardlink in Greece, the open space is mid-tier and cooperative banks.

patterns.Pattern: Consolidation in payments and acceptance is pushing players up the stack, from terminals into card issuing, acquiring, wallets, lending and orchestration. Software-only acceptance, known as SoftPOS, takes card payments on a phone and is eroding hardware POS. This widens the competitive front into Printec's adjacent acquiring and onboarding lines.

Euronet adds issuing (CoreCard), an A2A/IRIS wallet and >240,000 merchants via CrediaBank. Worldline/Cardlink pushes POS-as-cash-register, certified by AADE. Viva.com reported FY25 EUR258.6m, up 26%, and holds a full banking licence across 29 countries, including SK and SI.

Payten launched AI orchestration and AI merchant onboarding. Mellon extended to SoftPOS (NBG Pay, PayzyPOS) and IRIS, with 350k+ deployed and 500k+ supported across 9 countries. SoftPOS keeps replacing hardware POS (Payten N. Macedonia, Viva, myPOS/Advent).

Printec's POS, acquiring and TMS revenue faces two pressures at once. One is software-only erosion from SoftPOS. The other is full-stack acquirers that own issuing, acceptance and wallet together. AI-driven onboarding also encroaches on the eKYC/identity (Namirial) line.

The response is to bundle cash, card and managed services, a differentiator that rivals such as Loomis Pay are now copying. The second step is to partner up the stack rather than compete terminal by terminal.

patterns.Pattern: Digital platforms have reached scale, so the branch's role shifts to advice, and the shift is now mobile-first. Mobile banking is actively taking users from desktop and internet banking, not simply growing alongside it.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones): Serbia Q1-2026: m-banking users 5.34m (+10.3%) and m-banking transactions +28.1%, while e-banking transactions FELL -2.5% (users only +5.7%). North Macedonia: 71.7-71.8% of all electronically started payments go via mobile; mobile-enabled cards +~120% y/y. Montenegro mobile-payment users +45% vs internet +33% (end-2024). Ukraine ~85-91% of POS contactless, 18.6m tokenised cards. Greece's consumer access to instant payments rose from 33.0% to 62.4% (2022->2024, the fastest in the euro area).
patterns.What it means for Printec:
The endpoint that matters is the phone, not the branch PC. Build self-service, onboarding and acquiring around mobile and wallet rails: tokenisation, QR, SoftPOS, push-provisioning and app-to-ATM cardless withdrawal. Treat in-branch kiosks as bridges to the app.

Mobile-first transaction software and integration is structurally favoured over fixed-channel equipment. Freed branch capacity moves to advice.

patterns.Pattern: Remote and digital onboarding and eKYC (electronic identity checks) are moving from optional to mandatory. They are scaling on digital-identity rails such as the EUDI Wallet and national eIDs. They must now resist deepfakes, which makes verification a recurring managed defence rather than a one-off install.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
Under eIDAS 2.0, the EUDI Wallet must be available in every member state by end-2026. Bank acceptance becomes mandatory from Dec 2027. AMLR applies in full from Jul 2027.

Demand is scaling. Serbia recorded 139,244 distance financial-service contracts in Q1-2026 (+49.16%). Of these, 105,103 were electronic (+54.91%) and 34,141 used video-ID (+33.85%), while distance loans rose +112.7%. Ukraine's Diia (~23m users/~81% of adults) and Poland's mojeID (~22m) enable account opening.

There is a counter-force. Deepfake attacks occurred about every 5 min in 2024, and document forgeries rose +244%. Gartner flags that 30% of enterprises will view standalone IDV as unreliable by 2026, and only ~29% of onboarding data collection is AI-automated.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
A fixed regulatory deadline of Dec 2027 makes onboarding and eKYC a compliance requirement across the footprint. Ship a EUDI-Wallet relying-party connector.

Position eKYC as a continuously updated, layered liveness and anti-deepfake managed service, which produces recurring revenue. Broker bank-as-identity-provider deals in markets where the state wallet is late.

patterns.Pattern: AI is moving from assistant to operator in self-service and onboarding. The most durable and lowest-friction win is in operations and at the endpoint: predictive maintenance, fraud and AI-guided assisted service. Fully autonomous customer self-service is held back by a persistent preference for dealing with a human.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
NCR Atleos's AI service platform runs at fleet scale. It reports 95%+ diagnostic accuracy, a 13% global reduction in ATM service revisits, and a 50% drop in North America tech-support cases across 600,000+ ATMs.

Fraud offers the clearest return and is exempt from the EU AI Act's high-risk class. Credit scoring and biometric ID are treated differently and become high-risk from 02/08/2026. Banking AI software spend is rising from ~EUR31bn (2024) to ~EUR55bn (2027).

There is a limit. Capgemini finds gen-AI could save up to 66% of onboarding and operations time, yet 61% of customers still contact a human after a poor chatbot experience. That argues for assisted service rather than full automation.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
AI is a tailwind, not a threat. Sell 'AI-optimised availability' SLAs (service-level agreements) on the managed-services fleet, which means fewer revisits, higher uptime and higher margin. Sell AI fraud and video analytics at the endpoint, because they deploy fast and carry light regulation.

Position customer-facing AI as assisted, with a video-teller or copilot and a human fallback. AI that is compliant by design, logged and under human oversight is itself a reason to buy for CEE/SEE banks whose governance is behind.

patterns.Pattern: Western Europe is a delayed template, running 3-7yr ahead. Pooling and shared-ATM-utility models, IAD (independent ATM deployer) takeover of bank estates, and recycler retrofit on a shrinking fleet are the mechanisms that reach CEE/SEE next.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
Western European mechanisms are already consolidating fleets. Geldmaat in the Netherlands went from ~6,400 to 3,800 machines, and Bankomat in Sweden from 2,700 to 1,200, cutting cost by ~40%. Belgium's Batopin is retrofitting deposit capability to about half its cash points by 2026.

IADs rose from 16% to 18%+ of the Western European base, and recycling is 64% of automated-deposit ATMs. RBR flags pooling and IAD takeover as levers to 'watch spreading toward CEE/SEE'.

The footprint is behind the curve. Poland is the regional IAD anchor at 64% IAD-deployed, while SEE recycling is rare, with Serbia at 40 and Bulgaria at 8. UK free-to-use ATMs fell from 52,040 (2018) to 33,710 (2025), about -35%.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
The mature-market order book previews Printec's CEE/SEE pipeline. Position now as integrator and operator for emerging footprint pooling consortia, taking the role Auriga plays for Batopin. Bundle recyclers, managed services and monitoring, and white-label or operate IAD estates as banks pull back.

There is a multi-year runway, because the local estate is still flat to growing. Take the pooling, recycler and ATMaaS positions before the decline arrives.

patterns.Pattern: A regulatory and resilience floor is being written into law under the self-service and cash estate. Cash-access mandates and payment-resilience rules protect a minimum machine network by law, exactly where banks would otherwise cut. That reduces the risk in the installed base.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
Hungary's constitutional right to pay in cash, dated 14/04/2025, together with Act XVIII, requires ATMs in every municipality, with fines of HUF 2-200m. This drove the fleet above 5,500 by Dec 2025 even as withdrawals fell -9.4%. Per-bank allocations were gazetted, for example OTP 428 and MBH 195.

The EU Single Currency Package (Council 19/12/2025) requires 'sufficient and effective access to cash', with ATM geographic standards and a cash-acceptance mandate. Greece introduced an ATM-fee ban/cap of EUR1.50 on 11/08/2025.

National backstops exist as well: DNB 5km, UK LINK 1km plus 184 banking hubs, and Batopin/Geldmaat. Resilience forms a second floor. Ukraine runs a ~2,400-branch Power Banking network, and Sweden and Norway paused their cashless drive.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Where mandates apply, the minimum network is guaranteed demand, even at low-volume or rural sites. This favours banking-hub and shared self-service infrastructure, low-cost outsourced run-and-maintain, and resilient, power-independent self-service terminals (SST) with telemetry.

The mandate turns a shrinking cost line into a guaranteed-network duty that Printec can run as a service. The Greek fee cap in particular speeds the shift to recycler and ATMaaS economics.

patterns.Pattern: Serbia is different, because its physical network stays structurally stable while peers shrink. Country-specific cash culture, tourism and policy decide whether a fleet grows or shrinks, rather than the regional average. Neighbouring markets therefore diverge sharply.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
Serbia has the footprint's strongest reluctance to go off-site, at only 37% off-site, which means a preference for through-the-wall (TTW) machines. It has among CEE's highest withdrawals per ATM at ~2,734/month, and the fleet returned to +3.6% growth (Q1-2026, 3,336). Branches are down -24% since 2015, yet the network is resilient.

Within CEE-EU to 2028 the picture splits. The growers are Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania and Serbia. The decliners are Bulgaria (-1.7%, fastest fall) and Croatia (-1.1%), although Croatia was the only footprint country that added branches in 2025.

Greece shows ATMs +15.3%, driven by off-site and IAD deployment, while withdrawals fell -6.6%. Romania is the only primary CEE market with flat withdrawals (+0.5%) alongside +39% POS.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Density, withdrawals per machine and the grow-or-shrink call must be read country by country, not by region.

Romania, Serbia and the tourism markets justify recyclers, because cash volume there is resilient. Hungary's mandated rural fleet runs low volumes, so sell low-cost managed operations. Bulgaria, Croatia and Czechia are consolidation and replacement markets. The same product needs a different sales pitch in each country.

patterns.Pattern: Non-EU SEE is being brought to EU standards by policy and infrastructure years before membership, through SEPA, instant rails and anti-cash mandates. It is a build-out opportunity rather than a rationalisation one, on a timeline that is already set out in the calendar.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
SEPA accession is a fact for 4 of the 6 WB6 countries. AL, ME and MK went live in Oct 2025, and Serbia becomes operational in May 2026. The shared Banca d'Italia TIPS-clone goes live ~mid-2026 for AL/BiH/Kosovo/ME.

Albania's 2026 fiscal package requires POS for all taxpayers by 31/12/2026, under 'Cashless Albania 2030', with a target of >=60% digital by 2028.

Acceptance is building fast. Serbia POS grew +10.3% to 187,957 and Albania POS +27.7% to 31,263. Kosovo POS grew +21.4%, and only 6.7% of account-holding businesses have a terminal, which is the clearest greenfield opportunity. The EU Growth Plan (EUR6bn 2024-2027) funds it.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
There is a multi-year POS, SoftPOS and acquiring runway, plus dated SEPA and TIPS integration windows. These pull in Printec's payments, ISO 20022, fraud/AML, HSM and onboarding lines.

Sequence the work by readiness. Serbia and N. Macedonia lead on POS, acquiring and software. Albania moves fastest on policy, with POS and onboarding to 2028. Bosnia and Kosovo lag, so they come later but offer a bigger catch-up.

patterns.Pattern: Euro adoption moving east is a recurring, deadline-driven conversion event. Each accession triggers a full ATM, POS and cash-cycle reconfiguration on a fixed timetable. A rationalisation phase then follows the changeover.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
The pipeline is staged. Croatia joined in 2023, with ~70% of ATMs dispensing EUR on day 1 and all within 15 days. Bulgaria became the 21st euro member on 01/01/2026, with full cutover by 01/02/2026. Free exchange ends 30/06/2026, and the IPR is pinned to 01/01/2027. Romania targets ~2029-2030, and that date is slipping.

Post-changeover rationalisation is visible. Bulgaria's branches fell -10.7% in 2025, its euro-prep year and the sharpest cut in the EU. Its ATM base is forecast to fall fastest among CEE primaries, at -1.7% CAGR to 2028. The ECB June-2026 Convergence Report finds no next adopter is imminent, with Czechia closest but not in ERM II.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Euro-conversion projects are repeatable, calendar-locked revenue across Printec's full stack: hardware reconfiguration, software, integration and managed services. The Croatia to Bulgaria reference can be reused directly for Romania at ~2029-2030.

Plan for a demand pulse followed by post-euro fleet rationalisation, as seen in Bulgaria. Prepare the recycler and managed-services follow-on, not only the changeover spike.

patterns.Pattern: Ukraine is a one-of-a-kind market where war resilience, rather than cash culture or maturity, is the lasting driver of demand. It has a flat but critical self-service estate, energy-independent banking, a large recycler-upgrade gap, and a reconstruction wave that comes later.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
Through 4 years of war the ATM fleet has stayed stable at ~15.6-15.8k, down -0.6% in 2025. It has been maintained rather than expanded, while digital use raced ahead. Cashless is 96% by count and 67.3% by value, and POS is 558k+ with 90.9% contactless.

The NBU requires ATMs to be pre-stocked against outages. Power Banking covers ~2,400 energy-independent branches, about 75% of systemic banks, with national ATM roaming and a Diia filter.

Deposit and recycling capability is only 17.8% of the fleet, leaving ~13,000 dispense-only upgrade candidates. Branches keep shrinking, at 4,934 in Oct-2025 with 744 suspended. A reconstruction need of ~USD588bn over 10 years frames a re-equipment cycle that depends on a ceasefire.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Demand pulls toward resilient, energy-independent self-service, and toward ATM telemetry and remote monitoring across a roaming fleet. Recycler and intelligent-deposit upgrades follow, and PrivatBank is an existing NCR-recycler reference. Field and managed services plus security and compliance complete the offer, which gives a resilience angle unique in CEE.

The large reconstruction upside is real but arrives later, around 2028+. Treat it as a scenario, not a forecast.

patterns.Pattern: State-owned banks, post offices and central banks run the only publicly visible ATM and POS procurement. Commercial banks buy directly, away from the tender portals. The visible tender pipeline therefore understates real demand and points to the wrong buyers.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
This is a structural finding across markets. There are zero commercial-bank ATM/POS notices on EKR (Hungary), NEN/E-ZAK (Czechia), UVO (Slovakia), e-narocanje (Slovenia), EOJN (Croatia), UJN (Serbia) or SICAP (Romania, for BCR/BRD/BT). The finding is explicitly 'structural, not a coverage gap'.

Buyers using the public route fall into three groups. Central banks include the HNB cash-equipment cluster, BNB, BNR and NBS, which are mostly G+D-locked. State banks include CEC on its own portal, plus Ukraine's Oschadbank and PrivatBank on Prozorro. Posts include Bulgarian Post, with a 9.5M BGN euro programme, Posta Romana, Slovenska/Slovenije posta and Posta Srbije.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Watching portals is necessary, but it covers only a minority of demand. Split the coverage into two streams.

Run a scripted portal watch for the state, post and central-bank slice, where Printec can bid on open tenders. Run a named-account business-development push for commercial banks through the NCR Atleos channel. Posts, including ELTA and the Bulgarian, Romanian, Slovenian and Serbian posts, are a rising class of banking-channel buyers that tender publicly.

patterns.Pattern: Hardware demand is a replacement-cycle business, not a growth business. Re-fleeting dominates shipments, while the net installed base stays flat or declines.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
RBR reports that in CEE replacements were 84% of shipments (2023), rising to ~89% by 2028. The installed base peaked at ~256k (2013) and drifts to 231,895 by 2028 (-1.8%/yr).

Footprint refresh programmes confirm this. CEC Bank (RO) replaced ~1,100 and then >1,400 units, 'until the entire network is modernized'. PrivatBank (UA) bought 1,200 ATMs in 2025 and confirmed 800 in 2026, swapping fully depreciated machines for recyclers. Printec's 1,140-unit/838.6M UAH NCR contract is the incumbency anchor there.

Elsewhere, CSOB has ~230 of ~1,000 machines recycling (+~20%/yr). Slovak deposit-ATM fleets are growing: SLSP ~280, Tatra ~294 and VUB ~146.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Addressable ATM revenue is overwhelmingly recurring re-fleet and maintenance, rather than greenfield. The durable play is to defend incumbency and capture refreshes on machines reaching end of life, using NCR recyclers, x-core multivendor software, telemetry, OptiCash and managed or field services.

Measure each fleet's age profile to time refresh bids, instead of chasing net-new volume the market is not producing. A shrinking base still generates large, steady shipment demand.

patterns.Pattern: Leading indicators appear before the tender. Leadership appointments and 3+ concurrent role clusters in architecture, PMO, cards and cash operations signal channel and platform programmes ~6-12 months ahead. Bank M&A releases a fleet-standardisation budget 6-24 months after close.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones):
The operating rule is that a bank crosses a 'program threshold' at 3+ similar roles. Architecture, PMO and procurement hires come ~6-12mo before vendor selection.

Examples include Banca Transilvania's 'Enterprise Architect-Cards Domain', and CEOs or COOs with a digital mandate at SLSP, CIB, ING Romania, NBG Cyprus and NLB. Cash-operations and ATM-specialist roles include a Raiffeisen RS recycling-device handler and a Hipotekarna ME 'ATM specijalista'.

Mergers are the second trigger. Cyprus had three back-to-back deals with post-merger hiring clusters:
- Hellenic to Eurobank: 12/2025
- AstroBank to Alpha: 10/2025
- BoC to CDBbank: H2-2026

Intesa absorbed First Bank RO (~700 ATMs incl. Euronet). Nova KBM and SKB became one OTP (~450 ATMs). NLB and RBI are competing for Addiko across 5 SEE markets, with a decision ~22/07/2026.
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Get in position before an RFP exists. Approach the new digital or operations sponsor's office during the planning window, rather than after the tender is published, when incumbents are entrenched.

Each merger freezes standalone spend, then releases a standardisation and migration budget. Those are prime windows for x-core multivendor software to unify mixed NCR/Diebold fleets, unified telemetry, OptiCash, TMS rationalisation and IMTF/FICO AML re-screening.

Keep a hiring and M&A tracker for each market. One caveat: the counts come from aggregators and are point-in-time.

patterns.Pattern: A predictable baseline of demand recurs on fixed clocks. The central banks' yearly cash-equipment cycle and the service and maintenance re-tenders can be put in the diary and bid for ahead of time.
patterns.Evidence (see Metrics/Milestones): Contract-expiry triggers: Posta Romana Tezaur banking services on a 9-month term (re-tender ~mid-2026); BNR banknote-processing maintenance on ~annual cycles; the HNB 2026 Procurement Plan publishes a dated cash-equipment cluster (V-34 ~1.8M EUR supply Q4-2026, plus V-31/32/33/43/53 maintenance lots with quarters); Ukraine's Oschadbank/PrivatBank run continuous Prozorro lots (ATM parts, cash bags, recycler maintenance, ~95k EUR/yr); BPS/Posta Srbije recurring CIT + ATM servicing; banks reinforce ATMs each winter (UA Power Banking).
patterns.What it means for Printec:
Re-tender dates can be put in the diary and bid for ahead of time, rather than found late. Maintenance and managed-services renewals are the stickiest and highest-margin re-entry points, and incumbents are most exposed at the end of a contract.

One caveat: central-bank banknote-processing cores are largely G+D-locked. The contestable cycle is therefore teller, coin and sorting peripherals plus ATM-fleet service, not the high-speed central sorter.

outlook.scope: CrediaBank: sixteen branch conversions still to complete in 2026
outlook.summary:
CrediaBank has promised to convert 24 branches to its "New Experience" format by the end of 2026. That format is built around cash automation. At its half-year results, published on 6 August 2026, only eight conversions were complete. Sixteen branch fit-outs therefore have to be specified and delivered in the rest of the year, on a network that stays at 66 branches ([CrediaBank H1-2026 results presentation](https://www.crediabank.com/media/4p2kyv35/crediabank-i1-2026-financial-results-presentation-vf.pdf)).

The money is already disclosed and being spent, as part of a EUR 60m-plus digital transformation programme for 2026-2028. The bank's own specification asks for teller cash recyclers across the whole network. These are machines that re-use the notes customers have just paid in. Virtual teller stations are planned only at flagship sites, so there are two separate hardware lines to bid for.

Printec should aim at the in-branch cash and self-service fit-out, not at the ATM estate, which has been contracted out to Euronet. The digital instant loan due in October 2026 is a second, separate way in, through remote identity checks.
outlook.projected:
Growth, with most of it coming early. The triggers are dated, and the dates are close.

The half-year results published on 6 August 2026 confirm 24 branches due for conversion by end-2026. Only eight are complete. Six more are scheduled by early in the fourth quarter, and the remaining ten by year-end.

The Company Information Memorandum of 30 March 2026 says the bank plans to remodel the whole 66-branch network within two years. That leaves roughly 42 more sites for 2027-28. The same document names the same model for export to HSBC Malta's twelve branches.

The digital instant loan goes live in October 2026, which will need remote identity checks at scale. Customer Care launches in September 2026 and omnichannel in November 2026, either side of it ([CrediaBank H1-2026 results presentation](https://www.crediabank.com/media/4p2kyv35/crediabank-i1-2026-financial-results-presentation-vf.pdf)).

The limit to respect is scope. Euronet has exclusive rights over "ATM-related technical services" and CrediaBank's 141-machine ATM estate. That deal had still not closed as at 31 August 2026. There was no filing with the Hellenic Competition Commission, and no mention of CrediaBank in Euronet's second-quarter report ([Euronet Q2-2026 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1029199/000155485526001702/eeft-20260630.htm)).

Who to talk to: the CrediaBank branch-transformation and procurement owners. The topics are teller cash recyclers for the whole network, virtual teller stations for the flagship sites, card-on-entry customer recognition and accessibility kiosks. Work the October instant-loan launch separately. It is an electronic know-your-customer (identity check) conversation that sits fully outside the Euronet scope.

In short: the sixteen unbuilt conversions are the near-term contest. The roughly 42 sites behind them, plus the stated Malta export, are the reason to win the first one.
drivers: Only eight of the 24 planned "New Experience" branch conversions were complete at the half-year results published on 6 August 2026. Sixteen remain to be fitted out in the rest of 2026, on a network that stays at 66 branches ([CrediaBank H1-2026 results presentation](https://www.crediabank.com/media/4p2kyv35/crediabank-i1-2026-financial-results-presentation-vf.pdf)).

The bank has published its own specification, and it is built around cash automation. Customers are identified by bank card on entry, and cash transactions go through teller cash recyclers. Virtual teller stations link customers to staff through "CrediaConnect", and open collaboration areas replace the teller counter. Recyclers go network-wide, but virtual teller stations go only to flagship sites, so the two lines can be specified separately ([CrediaBank H1-2026 results presentation](https://www.crediabank.com/media/4p2kyv35/crediabank-i1-2026-financial-results-presentation-vf.pdf)).

Funding is disclosed and already being spent. There is a EUR 60m-plus Digital Transformation Programme for 2026-2028, with an 80-strong technology team. Half-year recurring operating expenses of EUR 76.7m are put down directly to the digital transformation and branch renovations ([CrediaBank H1-2026 results presentation](https://www.crediabank.com/media/4p2kyv35/crediabank-i1-2026-financial-results-presentation-vf.pdf)).

A dated digital timetable runs alongside the fit-outs. Customer Care is due in September 2026. The digital instant loan follows in October 2026, and omnichannel in November 2026. The loan launch will need remote identity checks at scale ([CrediaBank Company Information Memorandum, 30/03/2026](https://www.crediabank.com/media/sq2hz5w1/8-company-information-memorandum-30032026.pdf)).

Euronet's exclusive rights are worded around "ATM-related technical services" and cover the 141 ATMs. The deal was still not closed at 31 August 2026. There was no filing with the competition authority and no mention in the buyer's own quarterly report ([Euronet Q2-2026 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1029199/000155485526001702/eeft-20260630.htm)).
outlook.rationale:
The plan has not changed, but the reported numbers have. The bank published its own progress on 6 August 2026. The gap between what it promised for 2026 and what it has built is now sixteen branches, with only the rest of the year to close it. Those branches must be specified and ordered this quarter, or the year-end promise slips ([CrediaBank H1-2026 results presentation](https://www.crediabank.com/media/4p2kyv35/crediabank-i1-2026-financial-results-presentation-vf.pdf)).

At the same time, the final Euronet contract is still unsigned. The line between the ATM scope, which is closed off, and the in-branch cash and self-service scope is therefore easiest to argue right now ([Euronet Q2-2026 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1029199/000155485526001702/eeft-20260630.htm)). Once that deal closes, the argument gets harder.
cite_ungrounded: The "five months" framing is arithmetic from the 06/08/2026 results date to 31/12/2026, not a period the bank itself states.

Whether teller cash recyclers, virtual teller stations, entry recognition and accessibility kiosks fall outside Euronet's "ATM-related technical services" exclusivity is a reading of the clause, not a determination by either party to the agreement.
No supplier is named on any of the sixteen outstanding fit-outs; that the scope is unawarded is inferred from the absence of a disclosed supplier, not from a statement that it is open.

outlook.scope: ODAP Phase B visitor services, EUR 30m: award still to be decided
outlook.summary:
The Organisation for the Management and Development of Cultural Resources closed bids on 23 July 2026 for Phase B of digital visitor services at Greek archaeological sites and museums. An independent re-check of Greek notices on 27 August 2026 found no contract-award notice. The decision is therefore being made right now ([TED notice 408136-2026](https://ted.europa.eu/en/notice/408136-2026/xml)).

The notice gives a value of EUR 30,013,782.92. It does not say whether this includes value-added tax, so do not quote it either way.

The fit for Printec comes from the list of product codes. It includes ticket-issuing machines and point-of-sale software, alongside systems integration, across 108 existing Phase-A sites and 17 new ones. Printec's realistic role is a subcontract under whichever systems integrator wins. The value of this signal is knowing that the award is close, and reaching the likely lead bidders before it lands rather than after.
outlook.projected:
Growth, with little time to act. The open tender was published in the EU tenders journal as notice 408136-2026 on 15 June 2026. Bids closed on 23 July 2026. The re-check of Greek notices on 27 August 2026 found no award notice, so bids are being evaluated now. The award goes to the best price-quality ratio ([TED notice 408136-2026](https://ted.europa.eu/en/notice/408136-2026/xml)).

The scope adds to services already running at 108 Phase-A sites and extends them to 17 more. A Phase-A contract-change notice published 15 May 2026 shows a total contract value of EUR 23,202,224.50. That is the best guide to how the current supplier's work is shaped. This is the only Greek notice in the whole April-to-August 2026 window with a ticket-issuing-machine product code, so there is no similar second chance in this period.

Who to talk to: the systems integrators bidding for ODAP Phase B. The subject is the self-service ticketing kiosk, queue-management and card-acceptance parts of the lot, not leading the integration itself. Separately, talk to ODAP about the field-service, monitoring and cash-and-card operations layer that follows go-live across 125 visitor sites.

In short: get in position with the likely lead bidders in the weeks before the award is published. Once it is published, the subcontract structure is usually already fixed.
drivers: Bids closed on 23 July 2026, and no contract-award notice had been published as at 27 August 2026. The award decision is therefore still open at the time of writing ([TED notice 408136-2026](https://ted.europa.eu/en/notice/408136-2026/xml)).

The product codes include ticket-issuing machines and point-of-sale software alongside systems integration. This is the only Greek notice in the whole April-to-August 2026 window with a ticket-issuing-machine code ([TED notice 408136-2026](https://ted.europa.eu/en/notice/408136-2026/xml)).

The scope covers 108 Phase-A sites plus 17 new ones, 125 visitor locations in all. The award goes to the best price-quality ratio ([TED notice 408136-2026](https://ted.europa.eu/en/notice/408136-2026/xml)).

A Phase-A contract-change notice published on 15 May 2026 records a total contract value of EUR 23,202,224.50. That gives a concrete example of how the earlier phase was sized and delivered ([TED notice 408136-2026](https://ted.europa.eu/en/notice/408136-2026/xml)).
outlook.rationale: The requirement has not changed; the timing has. Bids closed on 23 July 2026, and the independent re-check on 27 August 2026 confirms that no award notice has appeared. That puts the programme in the short window where a lead bidder is still building its subcontractor list. After that, the list is fixed for the life of the contract ([TED notice 408136-2026](https://ted.europa.eu/en/notice/408136-2026/xml)). That window is the reason to act this month rather than next.
cite_ungrounded: The notice does not state whether EUR 30,013,782.92 is inclusive or exclusive of VAT, so any per-site or per-machine sizing derived from it is unsupported arithmetic.
The description of the 125 locations as high-footfall cash-and-card sites is inference from the scope, not language in the notice.
No bidder list is public, so identifying "plausible primes" has to be done from Greek market knowledge that sits outside this evidence base.
